input:
the two groups also differ in the pressure drop values that they report, and in the case of the benchmark material the difference between their respective values is larger than the repeatability that either group reports for its own measurements. The disagreement is rooted primarily in the test conditions employed, rather than in the material itself. One of the groups measured the pressure drop of the dry material, using a short bed and flow rates below those of the intended duty, and reported the bed in that state. The other group, by contrast, measured a bed already equilibrated with the vapour mixture, held at approximately the loading that the separation would operate at, and the pressure drop of the loaded bed was found to be higher on every run.

Part of the gap can be attributed to the bed itself, since the two groups did not draw their material from the same particle size fraction, and a bed of finer particles gives a higher pressure drop at the same flow rate, so some of the difference would be expected even between two dry beds measured in the same rig. The larger part, however, follows from the state of the material, in that a bed holding adsorbed vapour is a bed whose particles have swollen and whose void space has narrowed.

On balance, the values obtained from the equilibrated bed are preferred here, although this preference is a limited one. It rests on the duty for which the material is being assessed, since in service the benchmark material holds the vapour adsorbed on it, and the pressure drop that the plant will actually work against is that of the loaded bed rather than the dry one. For a duty involving a dry gas at low loading, the dry-bed values would represent the better basis, and the preference would be reversed.

The other group measured a bed equilibrated with the vapour mixture, held at about the loading the separation would run at, and the pressure drop of the loaded bed came out higher.

Part of the gap sits in the bed itself. The two groups did not draw their material from the same particle size fraction, and a bed of finer particles gives the higher pressure drop at the same flow, so some of the difference would appear even between two dry beds measured in the same rig. The larger part follows the state of the material: a bed holding adsorbed vapour is a bed whose particles have swollen and whose void space has narrowed, and its resistance to flow is the resistance of that narrower bed.

The preference here is for the values from the equilibrated bed, and the preference is a limited one. It rests on the duty the material is being assessed for: in service the benchmark material holds the vapour it has adsorbed, and the pressure drop the plant will work against is the pressure drop of the loaded bed, not of the dry one. For a duty on a dry gas at low loading the dry-bed values are the better basis, and on that condition the preference reverses.
